test.question: Under 1910.132(d)(1), what must the employer do before selecting PPE?
options: Buy the most expensive PPE available
Let each employee choose their own
Assess the workplace to determine if hazards are present, or likely to be present, that necessitate the use of PPE
Wait for an OSHA inspection
test.explanation: The employer must assess the workplace to determine whether hazards that require PPE are present or likely to be present. If they are, the employer must select PPE, communicate the selection to each affected employee, and select PPE that fits (1910.132(d)(1)). Workplace example: the safety coordinator walks the press line to identify flying-chip, noise, and pinch hazards before choosing PPE.

test.question: Under 1910.132(d)(2), how must the employer verify that the hazard assessment was performed?
options: A verbal statement from the safety manager at the next all-hands meeting that each work area has been walked through and the hazards and required PPE for each task reviewed with the crew
A photo of the work area
An entry on the OSHA 300 Log for each department, listing the hazards found in each work area, the PPE selected for each task, and the name of the supervisor who walked through the area
A written certification identifying the workplace evaluated, the person certifying, the date(s) of the assessment, and that the document is a certification of hazard assessment
test.explanation: The employer must verify the hazard assessment through a written certification that identifies the workplace evaluated, the person certifying the evaluation, the date(s) of the assessment, and identifies the document as a certification of hazard assessment (1910.132(d)(2)). Workplace example: a signed, dated "Certification of PPE Hazard Assessment - Machine Shop" is on file.

test.question: What does 1910.132(e) say about defective or damaged PPE?
options: It shall not be used
It may be used until a replacement arrives
It may be used for low-hazard tasks
It may be used if taped
test.explanation: Defective or damaged personal protective equipment shall not be used (1910.132(e)). Workplace example: a face shield with a cracked window is discarded, not used for the rest of the shift.

test.question: Which topic is NOT among the minimum PPE training items listed in 1910.132(f)(1)?
options: When PPE is necessary
The purchase price of the PPE
How to properly don, doff, adjust, and wear PPE
The limitations of the PPE
test.explanation: Each employee required to use PPE must be trained to know at least when PPE is necessary, what PPE is necessary, how to properly don, doff, adjust, and wear it, its limitations, and its proper care, maintenance, useful life, and disposal (1910.132(f)(1)). Price is not a training item. Workplace example: new hires practice fitting goggles and learn when face shields are required.

test.question: Under 1910.132(f)(2), what must each affected employee do before being allowed to perform work requiring PPE?
options: Sign a statement acknowledging that they received the PPE and accept responsibility for any injury from not using it
Buy their own PPE
Demonstrate an understanding of the training and the ability to use PPE properly
Watch the manufacturer's PPE video during orientation, then begin work in the area the same day
test.explanation: Each affected employee must demonstrate an understanding of the training and the ability to use PPE properly before being allowed to perform work requiring PPE (1910.132(f)(2)). Workplace example: the trainer watches each new employee put on and adjust a face shield and chemical gloves before they start at the plating line.

test.question: Which situation does 1910.132(f)(3) list as requiring PPE retraining?
options: Each employee's hiring anniversary, as an annual refresher on the same PPE they already use correctly
A new supervisor takes over the department, though the PPE, hazards, and employees' skills are all unchanged
The PPE is restocked from a new shipment of the identical model and size the employees already use
Changes in the types of PPE to be used make previous training obsolete
test.explanation: Retraining is required when the employer has reason to believe a trained employee lacks the required understanding or skill, including when workplace changes or changes in PPE types make previous training obsolete, or when inadequacies in the employee's knowledge or use show they have not retained it (1910.132(f)(3)(i)-(iii)). Workplace example: switching from cup goggles to indirect-vent goggles with different adjustment triggers retraining.

test.question: Under 1910.132(h)(2), which item is the employer NOT required to pay for?
options: Non-specialty safety-toe footwear that the employer permits to be worn off the job site
Chemical-resistant gloves
Face shields
Replacement for PPE that wore out in normal use, such as welding gloves with burned-through palms
test.explanation: The employer is not required to pay for non-specialty safety-toe protective footwear and non-specialty prescription safety eyewear, provided the employer permits them to be worn off the job site (1910.132(h)(2)). Other required PPE is provided at no cost (1910.132(h)(1)), including replacements unless lost or intentionally damaged (1910.132(h)(5)). Workplace example: the plant pays for welding gloves and face shields, but standard steel-toe boots may be the employee's cost.

test.question: Under 1910.133(a)(2), what must eye protection provide when there is a hazard from flying objects?
options: Tinted lenses
Side protection; detachable clip-on or slide-on side shields meeting the section are acceptable
Prescription lenses
Front impact protection only; side shields are needed only when the worker also wears prescription glasses
test.explanation: Each affected employee must use eye protection that provides side protection when there is a hazard from flying objects. Detachable side protectors such as clip-on or slide-on side shields are acceptable (1910.133(a)(2)). Workplace example: a machinist at a lathe throwing chips wears safety glasses with side shields.

test.question: Per the filter lens table in 1910.133(a)(5), what is the minimum protective shade for shielded metal arc welding with 5-8/32-inch electrodes at 160-250 amps?
options: Shade 7
Shade 8 minimum
Shade 10
Shade 12 minimum
test.explanation: The table lists a minimum protective shade of 10 for shielded metal arc welding with electrode size 5-8 (in 1/32 in.) and arc current 160-250 amps (1910.133(a)(5)). Workplace example: a welder running 3/16-inch (6/32) rod at 200 amps uses at least a shade 10 lens.

test.question: Under 1910.135(a)(2), what kind of helmet is required for an employee working near exposed electrical conductors that could contact the head?
options: Any bump cap
A metal helmet
A vented Class C hard hat
A protective helmet designed to reduce electrical shock hazard
test.explanation: The employer must ensure that a protective helmet designed to reduce electrical shock hazard is worn by each affected employee near exposed electrical conductors that could contact the head (1910.135(a)(2)). Helmets are also required where there is a potential for head injury from falling objects (1910.135(a)(1)). Workplace example: an electrician working below an overhead busway wears an electrically rated hard hat.

test.question: Under 1910.136(a), when must employees use protective footwear?
options: Where there is a danger of foot injuries from falling or rolling objects or objects piercing the sole, or where footwear protects against a remaining electrical hazard
Only in cold weather
Only in office areas
Only when the employee requests it
test.explanation: Protective footwear is required where there is a danger of foot injuries from falling or rolling objects or objects piercing the sole, or where protective footwear will protect the employee from an electrical hazard, such as static discharge or electric shock, that remains after other protective measures (1910.136(a)). Workplace example: warehouse workers moving drums on hand trucks wear safety-toe boots.

test.question: Under 1910.138(b), on what must the employer base the selection of hand protection?
options: The lowest price
An evaluation of the hand protection's performance characteristics relative to the tasks, conditions present, duration of use, and the hazards and potential hazards identified
The color the employee prefers
The glove listed in section 8 of the safety data sheet for the main solvent handled, issued in one style and size to every worker for every task in the department whatever the duration of use
test.explanation: Selection must be based on an evaluation of the performance characteristics of the hand protection relative to the tasks, conditions present, duration of use, and the hazards and potential hazards identified (1910.138(b)). Hand protection is required for hazards such as skin absorption, severe cuts, punctures, chemical and thermal burns (1910.138(a)). Workplace example: for an 8-hour solvent-wiping task, gloves are chosen by breakthrough time, not just "chemical resistant" on the box.

test.question: Under 1910.36(b)(1), how many exit routes must generally be available in a workplace?
options: At least one, with a second route added whenever more than 25 employees work on the same floor of the building
At least three
At least two, located as far apart as practical, except where 1910.36(b)(3) permits a single route
One exit route for every 50 employees on a shift, rounded up, with a single route allowed for smaller crews
test.explanation: At least two exit routes must be available to permit prompt evacuation, located as far away as practical from each other so one remains usable if the other is blocked, except as allowed in 1910.36(b)(3) (1910.36(b)(1)). Workplace example: the fabrication shop has exits at opposite ends of the building.

test.question: Under 1910.36(d)(1), how must employees be able to open an exit route door from the inside?
options: With a key kept in a break-glass box mounted beside each exit door
Only during business hours
With a keypad code
At all times, without keys, tools, or special knowledge
test.explanation: Employees must be able to open an exit route door from the inside at all times without keys, tools, or special knowledge. A panic bar that locks only from the outside is permitted on exit discharge doors (1910.36(d)(1)). Workplace example: the back dock door is fitted with panic hardware instead of a padlocked hasp.

test.question: Under 1910.36(e)(2), when must a door connecting a room to an exit route swing out in the direction of exit travel?
options: When the room is designed to be occupied by more than 50 people or is a high hazard area
Always
Only in buildings over three stories
Only when the room has a single door leading to the exit route
test.explanation: The door must swing out in the direction of exit travel if the room is designed for more than 50 people or is a high hazard area, meaning its contents are likely to burn with extreme rapidity or explode (1910.36(e)(2)). Workplace example: the doors from the 80-person training room swing outward into the corridor.

test.question: Under 1910.36(g)(1), what is the minimum ceiling height of an exit route?
options: 6 feet 8 inches
7 feet above finished floor
7 feet 6 inches
8 feet in production areas
test.explanation: The ceiling of an exit route must be at least 7 feet 6 inches high, and no projection from the ceiling may reach lower than 6 feet 8 inches from the floor (1910.36(g)(1)). Workplace example: a new duct run is kept above 6 feet 8 inches in the exit corridor.

test.question: Under 1910.36(g)(2), what is the minimum width of an exit access at all points?
options: 22 inches
28 inches
36 inches
44 inches
test.explanation: An exit access must be at least 28 inches wide at all points (1910.36(g)(2)). Objects projecting into the route may not reduce it below the minimum width (1910.36(g)(4)). Workplace example: racking along the aisle to the exit leaves at least 28 inches clear.

test.question: Which does 1910.37(a)(3) prohibit?
options: Lighting the exit route so an employee with normal vision can see along it, with fixtures mounted on the corridor walls and ceiling along its length
Marking each exit with a sign reading "Exit" in letters at least 6 inches high, illuminated by a reliable light source of at least 5 foot-candles
Fire doors on exits
Placing materials or equipment in the exit route, even temporarily, or routing the exit access through a room that can be locked
test.explanation: Exit routes must be free and unobstructed. No materials or equipment may be placed in the exit route, permanently or temporarily, and the exit access may not go through a room that can be locked, such as a bathroom, or lead into a dead-end corridor (1910.37(a)(3)). Workplace example: a pallet of returns staged in the exit corridor "for an hour" is not allowed.

test.question: Under 1910.37(b)(5), how must a doorway along an exit access that could be mistaken for an exit be marked?
options: "Not an Exit" or similar, or with a sign showing its actual use (e.g., "Closet")
It needs no marking
With a red light mounted above the door frame so it can be seen from the far end of the corridor
With an illuminated "Exit" sign and an arrow, so employees can use it when the main exit is blocked
test.explanation: Each doorway or passage along an exit access that could be mistaken for an exit must be marked "Not an Exit" or similar, or identified by a sign indicating its actual use, such as closet (1910.37(b)(5)). Workplace example: the storage room door beside the exit corridor gets a "Storage - Not an Exit" sign.

test.question: Under 1910.37(b)(7), how large must the letters in the word "Exit" be on an exit sign?
options: At least 4 inches high with 1/2-inch strokes
At least 6 inches high with principal strokes at least 3/4 inch wide
At least 8 inches high with principal strokes at least 1 inch wide, readable from 100 feet
Any legible size
test.explanation: Each exit sign must have the word "Exit" in plainly legible letters at least 6 inches high, with principal strokes at least 3/4 inch wide (1910.37(b)(7)). Signs must be illuminated to at least 5 foot-candles by a reliable source, or be self-luminous at the listed luminance (1910.37(b)(6)). Workplace example: a hand-lettered paper "EXIT" sign is replaced with a compliant illuminated sign.

test.question: Under 1910.38(b), when may an emergency action plan be communicated orally instead of in writing?
options: When there are 20 or fewer employees
When the employer has 50 or fewer employees
When the employer has 10 or fewer employees
When the building has sprinklers
test.explanation: An emergency action plan must be in writing, kept in the workplace, and available for review. An employer with 10 or fewer employees may communicate the plan orally (1910.38(b)). Workplace example: a 7-person machine shop reviews its plan verbally at hire.

test.question: Which is NOT one of the minimum elements of an emergency action plan under 1910.38(c)?
options: Procedures for reporting a fire or other emergency
Procedures to account for all employees after evacuation
The name or job title of every employee who can be contacted for more information
A list of the building's insurance carriers
test.explanation: Minimum elements are: procedures for reporting a fire or other emergency; procedures for emergency evacuation, including type of evacuation and exit route assignments; procedures for employees who remain to operate critical operations; procedures to account for all employees after evacuation; procedures for employees performing rescue or medical duties; and the name or job title of contacts for more information (1910.38(c)). Insurance carriers are not an element. Workplace example: the plan names the EHS coordinator and sets the head-count point in the north lot.

test.question: Under 1910.38(f), when must an employer review the emergency action plan with each covered employee?
options: When the plan is developed or the employee is first assigned to a job, when the employee's responsibilities under the plan change, and when the plan is changed
Within 90 days after the plan is developed or the employee is hired, then once each year at the annual safety meeting, with a short refresher after every evacuation drill
Only after an emergency
Only when OSHA requests it
test.explanation: The plan must be reviewed with each covered employee when the plan is developed or the employee is initially assigned to a job, when the employee's responsibilities under the plan change, and when the plan is changed (1910.38(f)(1)-(3)). Workplace example: an employee newly assigned as an evacuation warden gets a review of the warden duties.

test.question: Which is a required element of a fire prevention plan under 1910.39(c)?
options: The company's annual revenue
Procedures to control accumulations of flammable and combustible waste materials
Procedures to account for all employees after an emergency evacuation, including a head count at each assembly point
The names of all customers
test.explanation: A fire prevention plan must include a list of major fire hazards with handling and storage procedures, ignition sources and their control, and needed fire protection equipment; procedures to control accumulations of flammable and combustible waste; procedures for maintaining safeguards on heat-producing equipment; and the names or job titles of employees responsible for ignition-source equipment and for fuel source hazards (1910.39(c)(1)-(5)). Workplace example: the plan sets a daily schedule for emptying oily-rag cans in the paint shop.

title: Portable Fire Extinguishers
topics: Monthly visual inspection and annual maintenance

resources.title: Portable Fire Extinguishers Standard
resources.description: Full text of 29 CFR 1910.157 on osha.gov

resources.title: eCFR: 29 CFR 1910.157
resources.description: Current official text of the portable fire extinguishers standard

resources.title: Fire Safety Topic Page
resources.description: OSHA overview and guidance on workplace fire safety

test.question: Under 1910.157(c)(1), how must the employer mount, locate, and identify portable fire extinguishers?
options: In a locked cabinet near the office
Only at building exits
So they are readily accessible to employees without exposing employees to possible injury
Anywhere, as long as there is one per floor
test.explanation: The employer must provide portable fire extinguishers and mount, locate, and identify them so they are readily accessible to employees without exposing them to possible injury (1910.157(c)(1)). Workplace example: an extinguisher behind stacked pallets is moved to a marked, clear wall bracket.

test.question: Which extinguishing agents does 1910.157(c)(3) prohibit in the workplace?
options: Carbon dioxide and Halon 1211 in rooms with energized electrical equipment
Water and foam
Halon 1211 and Halon 1301
Carbon tetrachloride and chlorobromomethane
test.explanation: The employer may not provide or make available portable fire extinguishers that use carbon tetrachloride or chlorobromomethane extinguishing agents (1910.157(c)(3)). Workplace example: an old carbon tetrachloride unit found in a storeroom is removed from the workplace.

test.question: Under 1910.157(c)(4), in what condition and where must portable fire extinguishers be kept?
options: Fully charged and operable, and kept in their designated places at all times except during use
At least half charged, as shown by the gauge, and left at the spot where they were last used until recharged
Empty until a fire occurs
Stored in the maintenance shop between monthly inspections, and brought out only when hot work is under way
test.explanation: Portable fire extinguishers must be maintained fully charged and operable and kept in their designated places at all times except during use (1910.157(c)(4)). Workplace example: an extinguisher used on a small trash fire is replaced right away, not left empty on its hook.

test.question: Under 1910.157(d)(2), what is the maximum travel distance from an employee to an extinguisher for Class A fires?
options: 50 feet
75 feet
100 feet
150 feet
test.explanation: Extinguishers for Class A fires must be distributed so the travel distance for employees to any extinguisher is 75 feet or less (1910.157(d)(2)). Workplace example: in a 300-foot warehouse aisle, extinguishers are spaced so no one is more than 75 feet from one.

test.question: Under 1910.157(d)(4), what is the maximum travel distance from a Class B hazard area to an extinguisher?
options: 25 feet
50 feet
75 feet
100 feet
test.explanation: Extinguishers for Class B fires must be distributed so the travel distance from the Class B hazard area to any extinguisher is 50 feet or less (1910.157(d)(4)). Workplace example: a Class B extinguisher is mounted within 50 feet of the solvent dip tank.

test.question: Under 1910.157(d)(5), how are extinguishers for Class C hazards distributed?
options: One per electrical panel
Within 25 feet of every outlet
Only in server rooms
On the basis of the appropriate pattern for the existing Class A or Class B hazards
test.explanation: Portable fire extinguishers for Class C hazards must be distributed on the basis of the appropriate pattern for the existing Class A or Class B hazards (1910.157(d)(5)). Workplace example: the extinguishers near the motor control center follow the Class A or B spacing already used in that area.

test.question: How often must portable extinguishers be visually inspected under 1910.157(e)(2)?
options: Monthly
Weekly
Quarterly
Annually
test.explanation: Portable extinguishers, or hose used in their place under (d)(3), must be visually inspected monthly (1910.157(e)(2)). Workplace example: on the first workday of each month, a designated employee checks each unit's gauge, pin, and seal.

test.question: What does 1910.157(e)(3) require for the annual maintenance check?
options: The employer must record the annual check and keep the record for three years
The employer must record the annual maintenance date and keep the record for one year after the last entry or the life of the shell, whichever is less
The record must be kept for 30 years
Stored pressure extinguishers need an internal exam every year
test.explanation: Portable extinguishers must get an annual maintenance check. Stored pressure extinguishers do not require an internal examination. The employer must record the annual maintenance date and keep the record for one year after the last entry or the life of the shell, whichever is less (1910.157(e)(3)). Workplace example: the service company dates the tag, and the tag stays on the unit as the record.

test.question: Under 1910.157(e)(4), stored pressure dry chemical extinguishers that require a 12-year hydrostatic test must be emptied and given maintenance every:
options: 3 years
5 years
6 years
10 years
test.explanation: Stored pressure dry chemical extinguishers that require a 12-year hydrostatic test must be emptied and given the applicable maintenance every 6 years. Non-refillable disposable units are exempt, and the 6-year clock restarts after recharging or hydrostatic testing (1910.157(e)(4)). Workplace example: an ABC unit last recharged in 2020 is due for its 6-year teardown in 2026.

test.question: Per Table L-1 in 1910.157(f)(2), how often must carbon dioxide extinguishers be hydrostatically tested?
options: Every 6 years
Every 10 years
Every 12 years
Every 5 years
test.explanation: Table L-1 lists carbon dioxide extinguishers at a 5-year hydrostatic test interval (1910.157(f)(2) Table L-1). 1910.157(f)(10) also requires carbon dioxide extinguishers to be tested every 5 years at 5/3 of the stamped service pressure. Workplace example: CO2 units in the electrical room are sent out for hydrostatic testing on a 5-year cycle.

test.question: What does 1910.157(e)(5) require when extinguishers are removed from service for maintenance or recharging?
options: Alternate equivalent protection must be provided
Nothing; the area can go without for up to a week
Work in the area must stop
Only a sign must be posted
test.explanation: When portable fire extinguishers are removed from service for maintenance and recharging, the employer must provide alternate equivalent protection (1910.157(e)(5)). Workplace example: the service vendor leaves loaner units on the hooks while the plant's extinguishers are being recharged.

test.question: Under 1910.157(g)(1)-(2), when the employer provides extinguishers for employee use, when must the educational program be given?
options: Upon initial employment only, with a refresher when extinguishers are replaced
Upon initial employment and at least annually thereafter
Upon initial employment and at least every three years thereafter
Only to the fire brigade
test.explanation: Where extinguishers are provided for employee use, the employer must provide an educational program on the general principles of extinguisher use and the hazards of incipient-stage firefighting (1910.157(g)(1)), upon initial employment and at least annually thereafter (1910.157(g)(2)). Workplace example: new hires get the extinguisher briefing in orientation, and all employees get a refresher each year.

title: Permit-Required Confined Spaces
topics: What makes a space a confined space
Evaluating the workplace and posting signs
Entry permits: signing, cancelling, and retaining

resources.title: Permit-Required Confined Spaces Standard
resources.description: Full text of 29 CFR 1910.146 on osha.gov

resources.title: eCFR: 29 CFR 1910.146
resources.description: Current official text of the permit-required confined spaces standard

resources.title: Confined Spaces Topic Page
resources.description: OSHA overview and guidance on confined spaces

test.question: Under the definitions in 1910.146(b), which set of conditions makes a space a "confined space"?
options: Large enough for an employee to bodily enter and work, designed for continuous employee occupancy, and containing or having the potential to contain a hazardous atmosphere or engulfment hazard
Any space below grade
Large enough and configured for an employee to bodily enter and work, limited or restricted means of entry or exit, and not designed for continuous employee occupancy
Any space with a single entry point and less than 100 square feet of floor area that an employee can reach into with arms and tools, even if it is too small for the employee to bodily enter
test.explanation: A confined space is large enough and configured so an employee can bodily enter and perform work, has limited or restricted means of entry or exit, and is not designed for continuous employee occupancy (1910.146(b)). A permit-required confined space is a confined space that also has one or more listed hazards. Workplace example: a product storage hopper meets all three conditions.

test.question: What is the employer's first duty under 1910.146(c)(1)?
options: Buy a gas meter
Train every employee as an entrant
Hire a rescue service
Evaluate the workplace to determine whether any spaces are permit-required confined spaces
test.explanation: The employer must evaluate the workplace to determine whether any spaces are permit-required confined spaces (1910.146(c)(1)). Workplace example: the plant surveys its tanks, pits, and vaults and lists which are permit spaces.

test.question: How does 1910.146(c)(2) require employers to inform exposed employees of permit spaces?
options: By posting danger signs or by any other equally effective means; a sign reading "DANGER--PERMIT-REQUIRED CONFINED SPACE, DO NOT ENTER" would satisfy it
By posting signs reading "CAUTION--CONFINED SPACE" at each entrance; the word DANGER is reserved for spaces where testing has measured an atmospheric hazard above the PEL
By training only the authorized entrants, attendants, and entry supervisors on space locations, since employees who never enter need not be told the spaces exist
By posting signs only at permit spaces entered at least once a year, while rarely entered spaces are covered by a note in the written program kept in the safety office
test.explanation: If the workplace has permit spaces, the employer must inform exposed employees of their existence, location, and danger by posting danger signs or other equally effective means. "DANGER--PERMIT-REQUIRED CONFINED SPACE, DO NOT ENTER" or similar language satisfies the sign requirement (1910.146(c)(2)). Workplace example: the sign is stenciled on each tank manway.

test.question: Under 1910.146(c)(4), what must the employer do if it decides its employees will enter permit spaces?
options: Issue each entrant a calibrated four-gas meter in place of a written program
Develop and implement a written permit space program that complies with 1910.146 and is available to employees and their representatives
Rely on a pre-entry checklist kept at each space and the entry supervisor's experience, so a written permit space program is needed only after an entry incident occurs
Get verbal approval from the plant manager before each entry and have the attendant log who entered and when, in place of a written permit space program
test.explanation: If employees will enter permit spaces, the employer must develop and implement a written permit space program complying with 1910.146, available for inspection by employees and their authorized representatives (1910.146(c)(4)). If employees will not enter, the employer must take effective measures to prevent entry (1910.146(c)(3)). Workplace example: the maintenance department's written program covers every tank it enters.

test.question: In what order does 1910.146(d)(5)(iii) require testing for atmospheric hazards?
options: Toxic gases and vapors first, then oxygen, then combustibles, since toxics such as H2S act fastest
Combustible gases and vapors first, then oxygen, then toxic gases and vapors, since fire or explosion is the most immediate danger
Oxygen first, then combustible gases and vapors, then toxic gases and vapors
Any order
test.explanation: When testing for atmospheric hazards, test first for oxygen, then combustible gases and vapors, then toxic gases and vapors (1910.146(d)(5)(iii)). Workplace example: the entry supervisor reads O2, then LEL, then H2S and CO from the meter at the manway.

test.question: Under 1910.146(e)(2), who must sign the entry permit before entry begins?
options: The attendant assigned to the space, after the entrants are ready
Any authorized entrant
The plant safety director only
The entry supervisor identified on the permit
test.explanation: Before entry begins, the entry supervisor identified on the permit must sign it to authorize entry (1910.146(e)(2)). The completed permit must be made available to entrants, such as by posting at the entry portal (1910.146(e)(3)). Workplace example: the supervisor signs the permit and clips it at the manway before anyone goes in.

test.question: Under 1910.146(e)(5), when must the entry supervisor terminate entry and cancel the permit?
options: When the entry operations covered by the permit are completed, or when a condition not allowed under the permit arises in or near the space
Only at the end of the week
Only if someone is injured
Only when the attendant leaves
test.explanation: The entry supervisor must terminate entry and cancel the permit when the covered entry operations are completed, or when a condition not allowed under the permit arises in or near the space (1910.146(e)(5)(i)-(ii)). Workplace example: when the blower trips, entrants are called out and the permit is cancelled.

test.question: How long must cancelled entry permits be kept under 1910.146(e)(6)?
options: 30 days
At least 1 year
3 years
30 years
test.explanation: Each cancelled entry permit must be retained for at least 1 year to support the program review required within 1 year after each entry (1910.146(d)(14)), and any problems during the entry must be noted on the permit (1910.146(e)(6)). Workplace example: cancelled permits are filed by month in the maintenance office and reviewed within a year of each entry.

test.question: Under 1910.146(g)(2), when must confined space training be provided to each affected employee?
options: Before the employee is first assigned duties and then annually in a classroom refresher; no new training is needed when duties or operations change if the employee has entered permit spaces before
Only after an incident
Before first assignment of duties, before a change in assigned duties, when operations change to present an untrained hazard, and when deviations or inadequacies in knowledge are suspected
Only to entry supervisors
test.explanation: Training must be given before the employee is first assigned duties, before a change in assigned duties, whenever a change in operations presents a hazard the employee has not been trained on, and whenever the employer has reason to believe there are deviations from procedures or inadequacies in knowledge (1910.146(g)(2)(i)-(iv)). Workplace example: a mechanic moving from attendant to entrant duties is trained before the new role.

test.question: What must the training certification under 1910.146(g)(4) contain?
options: Only the course title
Each employee's name, the employee's score on the written test, and the date the next refresher training is due
Only the trainer's certificate number
Each employee's name, the signatures or initials of the trainers, and the dates of training
test.explanation: The employer must certify that the required training has been done. The certification must contain each employee's name, the signatures or initials of the trainers, and the dates of training, and be available to employees and their representatives (1910.146(g)(4)). Workplace example: the training roster has each entrant's name, the trainer's initials, and the date.

test.question: Under 1910.146(i)(4), where must the attendant be during entry operations?
options: Outside the permit space until relieved by another attendant
Inside the permit space near the portal, where the entrants can be seen and heard
In the control room
Wherever needed to help the entrants, including inside the space for short tasks
test.explanation: The attendant must remain outside the permit space during entry operations until relieved by another attendant (1910.146(i)(4)), and may perform no duties that would interfere with monitoring and protecting the entrants (1910.146(i)(10)). Workplace example: the attendant stays at the manway with the radio and entry log for the whole entry.

test.question: Under 1910.146(k)(3)(ii), what must be available to retrieve personnel from vertical permit spaces more than 5 feet deep?
options: A ladder only
A mechanical device
A second entrant
An off-site rescue service on call instead
test.explanation: The other end of the retrieval line must be attached to a mechanical device or fixed point outside the space so rescue can begin as soon as it is needed, and a mechanical device must be available for vertical permit spaces more than 5 feet deep (1910.146(k)(3)(ii)). Workplace example: a tripod and winch are set up over a 10-foot-deep sump before entry.

title: Bloodborne Pathogens
topics: Written Exposure Control Plan and annual review

resources.title: Bloodborne Pathogens Standard
resources.description: Full text of 29 CFR 1910.1030 on osha.gov

resources.title: eCFR: 29 CFR 1910.1030
resources.description: Current official text of the bloodborne pathogens standard

resources.title: Bloodborne Pathogens Topic Page
resources.description: OSHA overview and guidance on bloodborne pathogens

test.question: Under 1910.1030(c)(1)(i), what must an employer with employees who have occupational exposure establish?
options: A verbal exposure control procedure reviewed with each employee at hire, with a written plan due after the first exposure incident
Only a first aid kit
A written Exposure Control Plan designed to eliminate or minimize employee exposure
A contract with a hospital
test.explanation: Each employer with employees who have occupational exposure must establish a written Exposure Control Plan designed to eliminate or minimize exposure (1910.1030(c)(1)(i)). Workplace example: a plant whose designated first aid responders may contact blood keeps a written plan.

test.question: How often must the Exposure Control Plan be reviewed and updated under 1910.1030(c)(1)(iv)?
options: Every three years, or sooner when the workers' compensation carrier or local health department identifies new tasks with occupational exposure
Only after an exposure incident
Only when OSHA revises the standard
At least annually, and whenever necessary to reflect new or modified tasks, procedures, or positions with occupational exposure
test.explanation: The plan must be reviewed and updated at least annually and whenever necessary to reflect new or modified tasks and procedures affecting exposure, or new or revised positions with occupational exposure (1910.1030(c)(1)(iv)). Workplace example: adding a new first aid team at the second shop triggers a plan update before the annual review.

test.question: What does 1910.1030(d)(1) require when it is difficult to tell body fluid types apart?
options: Observe universal precautions, and consider all body fluids potentially infectious materials
Treat only visible blood as infectious
Wait for lab results before cleanup
Treat the fluid as non-infectious
test.explanation: Universal precautions must be observed to prevent contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials. Where differentiating body fluid types is difficult or impossible, all body fluids must be considered potentially infectious materials (1910.1030(d)(1)). Workplace example: a responder treats a mixed fluid spill as infectious.

test.question: Under 1910.1030(d)(2)(v), when must employees wash their hands?
options: At the end of the shift
Immediately or as soon as feasible after removing gloves or other personal protective equipment
Only if blood is visible on the hands after glove removal; otherwise hand sanitizer at the end of the task is enough
Before putting on gloves and at the end of the shift, since wearing gloves keeps the hands from being contaminated during the task
test.explanation: Employers must ensure employees wash their hands immediately or as soon as feasible after removing gloves or other PPE (1910.1030(d)(2)(v)). Workplace example: after bandaging a coworker's cut, the responder removes gloves and washes right away.

test.question: What does 1910.1030(d)(2)(vii) say about contaminated needles and sharps?
options: They may be recapped by hand whenever convenient
They may be broken before disposal to save space
They may not be bent, recapped, or removed except as allowed in (A) and (B), and shearing or breaking them is prohibited
They may be thrown in regular trash if capped
test.explanation: Contaminated needles and other sharps may not be bent, recapped, or removed except as noted in (d)(2)(vii)(A) and (B), and shearing or breaking contaminated needles is prohibited (1910.1030(d)(2)(vii)). Under (A), bending, recapping, or removal is allowed only when no alternative is feasible or a specific medical or dental procedure requires it. Workplace example: the plant nurse drops used needles straight into a sharps container without recapping.

test.question: Under 1910.1030(d)(2)(ix), which activities are prohibited in work areas where occupational exposure is reasonably likely?
options: Wearing disposable gloves when hand contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials can be reasonably anticipated
Eating, drinking, and smoking only; applying lip balm and handling contact lenses are allowed if hands are washed first
Washing hands with antiseptic hand cleaner and towelettes when running water is not available at the work site
Eating, drinking, smoking, applying cosmetics or lip balm, and handling contact lenses
test.explanation: Eating, drinking, smoking, applying cosmetics or lip balm, and handling contact lenses are prohibited in work areas where there is a reasonable likelihood of occupational exposure (1910.1030(d)(2)(ix)). Workplace example: no coffee cups in the first aid room.

test.question: Under 1910.1030(f)(2)(i), when must hepatitis B vaccination be made available to employees with occupational exposure?
options: After they receive the required training and within 10 working days of initial assignment (unless an exception applies)
After their first exposure incident only, as part of the post-exposure evaluation rather than at initial assignment to the job
Within 90 days of initial assignment, after the employee completes a pre-vaccination antibody screening test at the employee's own expense
Only if they request it in writing
test.explanation: Hepatitis B vaccination must be made available after the employee receives the required training and within 10 working days of initial assignment, unless the employee already completed the series, antibody testing shows immunity, or the vaccine is contraindicated (1910.1030(f)(2)(i)). Workplace example: a newly designated first aid responder is offered the series within 10 working days.

test.question: An employee declines the hepatitis B vaccination. What does 1910.1030(f)(2)(iv) require?
options: The employee signs a declination, and the offer of vaccination is then permanently closed
The employee must sign the declination statement in Appendix A
The employee must be removed from the job
The employer must vaccinate anyway
test.explanation: Employees who decline hepatitis B vaccination must sign the statement in Appendix A (1910.1030(f)(2)(iv)). If the employee later decides to accept while still covered, the vaccination must be made available then (1910.1030(f)(2)(iii)). Workplace example: the signed declination is filed, and the offer stays open.

test.question: Under 1910.1030(g)(1)(i), what color must biohazard warning labels be, and what may substitute for labels?
options: Fluorescent yellow with black lettering and the biohazard symbol; clear bags may substitute if the contents are listed on an attached tag or form
Green; clear bags
Fluorescent orange or orange-red (or predominantly so) with contrasting lettering and symbols; red bags or red containers may substitute
Blue with white lettering and the biohazard symbol; any closed, leakproof container may substitute for a label if it is kept in a locked area
test.explanation: Labels must be fluorescent orange or orange-red, or predominantly so, with lettering and symbols in a contrasting color (1910.1030(g)(1)(i)(C)). Red bags or red containers may be substituted for labels (1910.1030(g)(1)(i)(E)). Workplace example: bloody gauze from first aid goes in a red bag.

test.question: When must bloodborne pathogens training be provided under 1910.1030(g)(2)?
options: At no cost, at initial assignment to tasks with possible exposure, and every three years thereafter; sessions may be held after working hours if employees are paid for the time
Within 90 days after initial assignment to tasks with possible exposure and every two years thereafter, with the training cost shared between the employer and each employee
Only to supervisors
At no cost, during working hours, at initial assignment to tasks with possible exposure, and at least annually thereafter (within one year of the previous training)
test.explanation: Training must be provided at no cost to the employee and during working hours (1910.1030(g)(2)(i)), at the time of initial assignment to tasks with possible occupational exposure, and at least annually thereafter (1910.1030(g)(2)(ii)). Annual training must be within one year of the previous training (1910.1030(g)(2)(iv)). Workplace example: first aid responders' refresher is scheduled each spring, on the clock.

test.question: How long must medical records for employees with occupational exposure be kept under 1910.1030(h)(1)(iv)?
options: For at least the duration of employment plus 30 years
3 years
5 years
Until the employee leaves
test.explanation: Medical records required by 1910.1030(h) must be kept for at least the duration of employment plus 30 years, in accordance with 1910.1020 (1910.1030(h)(1)(iv)). Training records are kept 3 years from the date of training (1910.1030(h)(2)(ii)). Workplace example: a responder's vaccination record stays on file for 30 years after they leave.

title: Injury and Illness Recordkeeping and Reporting

resources.title: General Recording Criteria
resources.description: When a work-related injury or illness must be recorded

resources.title: Reporting Severe Injuries to OSHA
resources.description: Fatality and severe injury reporting

resources.title: eCFR: 29 CFR Part 1904
resources.description: Current official text of the recordkeeping regulation

resources.title: Recordkeeping Topic Page
resources.description: OSHA recordkeeping forms and guidance

test.question: Under 1904.4(a), which conditions must all be met for a fatality, injury, or illness to be recorded?
options: It caused at least one lost workday
It is work-related, is a new case, and meets one or more of the general recording criteria (or the specific-case criteria)
The employee filed a workers' compensation claim
A physician saw the employee
test.explanation: Employers required to keep records must record each fatality, injury, and illness that is work-related, is a new case, and meets one or more of the general recording criteria in 1904.7 or the specific-case criteria in 1904.8-1904.12 (1904.4(a)). Workplace example: a new forklift-related sprain that needed prescription medication meets all three.

test.question: Under 1904.5(a), when must an injury or illness be considered work-related?
options: If an event or exposure in the work environment was the predominant cause; a pre-existing condition that is aggravated at work is excluded unless a physician confirms it
Only if a supervisor witnessed it
If an event or exposure in the work environment caused or contributed to it, or significantly aggravated a pre-existing injury or illness
Only if the employee was following procedures
test.explanation: An injury or illness is work-related if an event or exposure in the work environment caused or contributed to it or significantly aggravated a pre-existing condition. Work-relatedness is presumed for events or exposures in the work environment unless a 1904.5(b)(2) exception applies (1904.5(a)). Workplace example: a lifting strain on the dock is presumed work-related.

test.question: Which outcome makes a work-related case recordable under the general recording criteria in 1904.7(b)(1)?
options: First aid only
A visit to the nurse for observation only
A report of discomfort with no treatment
Medical treatment beyond first aid
test.explanation: A work-related injury or illness must be recorded if it results in death, days away from work, restricted work or transfer, medical treatment beyond first aid, loss of consciousness, or a significant injury or illness diagnosed by a physician or other licensed health care professional (1904.7(b)(1)(i)-(vi)). Workplace example: a cut closed with sutures is recordable; one cleaned and bandaged is not.

test.question: Under 1904.7(b)(5)(ii)(D), which wound treatment is medical treatment (and so recordable) rather than first aid?
options: Sutures or staples
Butterfly bandages on a deep cut
Steri-Strips on a laceration
Gauze pads and an elastic wrap
test.explanation: Wound coverings such as bandages, gauze pads, butterfly bandages, and Steri-Strips are first aid. Other wound-closing devices such as sutures and staples are medical treatment (1904.7(b)(5)(ii)(D)). Workplace example: a laceration closed with three stitches at urgent care is recorded.

test.question: When counting days away from work under 1904.7(b)(3)(iv), how are weekends and holidays treated?
options: They are not counted
All calendar days the employee was unable to work are counted, including weekends, holidays, and other days off
Only scheduled workdays are counted
Only weekdays are counted
test.explanation: Count the number of calendar days the employee was unable to work because of the injury or illness, whether or not they were scheduled to work. Weekends, holidays, vacation days, and other days off are included (1904.7(b)(3)(iv)). Counting starts the day after the injury (1904.7(b)(3)(i)). Workplace example: an employee hurt Thursday and off through the next Tuesday has 5 days away.

test.question: Under 1904.7(b)(3)(vii), at what point may the employer stop counting days away from work?
options: 90 calendar days (one quarter)
365 calendar days (one year)
180 calendar days
There is no cap
test.explanation: The employer may cap the total days away at 180 calendar days (1904.7(b)(3)(vii)). Workplace example: an employee off for 210 days after surgery is entered as 180 days away.

test.question: Under 1904.29(b)(3), how quickly must a recordable case be entered on the OSHA 300 Log and 301 Incident Report?
options: Within 24 hours
Within 30 days
By the end of the year
Within 7 calendar days of receiving information that it occurred
test.explanation: Each recordable injury or illness must be entered on the OSHA 300 Log and 301 Incident Report within seven calendar days of receiving information that it occurred (1904.29(b)(3)). Workplace example: a recordable case reported Monday must be logged by the following Monday.

test.question: Which of these must be treated as a privacy concern case under 1904.29(b)(7)?
options: A needlestick injury from a sharp contaminated with another person's blood or other potentially infectious material
A broken arm from a fall from a stepladder in the warehouse that required surgery, a hospital stay, and several weeks away from work
A back strain from lifting a patient that kept the employee off work for more than five days and required outpatient physical therapy
A burn from a hot pipe
test.explanation: Privacy concern cases include injuries to an intimate body part or the reproductive system, sexual assault, mental illnesses, HIV infection, hepatitis, or tuberculosis, needlesticks and cuts from sharps contaminated with another person's blood or OPIM, and other illnesses if the employee asks (1904.29(b)(7)(i)-(vi)). For these, enter "privacy case" instead of the name (1904.29(b)(6)). Workplace example: the plant nurse's contaminated needlestick is logged as "privacy case."

test.question: Under 1904.32(b)(4), which of these may NOT certify the annual summary as the "company executive"?
options: An officer of the corporation
The clerk who maintains the OSHA 300 Log
The highest ranking company official working at the establishment
The immediate supervisor of the highest ranking official at the establishment
test.explanation: The certifying company executive must be an owner (sole proprietorship or partnership only), an officer of the corporation, the highest ranking company official at the establishment, or that official's immediate supervisor (1904.32(b)(4)). The executive must certify that they examined the log and reasonably believe the summary is correct and complete (1904.32(b)(3)). Workplace example: the plant manager signs the 300-A, not the HR clerk who prepared it.

test.question: How long must the OSHA 300 Log, privacy case list, annual summary, and 301 forms be kept under 1904.33(a)?
options: 1 year
3 years following the end of the calendar year the records cover, then they may be discarded
5 years following the end of the calendar year the records cover
30 years
test.explanation: These records must be saved for five years following the end of the calendar year they cover (1904.33(a)). Stored 300 Logs must be updated during that period for newly discovered cases and classification changes (1904.33(b)(1)). Workplace example: the 2026 log is kept through the end of 2031.

test.question: Under 1904.39(a)(2), within what time must an employer report a work-related in-patient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye to OSHA?
options: 8 hours
24 hours
72 hours (3 days)
7 days
test.explanation: In-patient hospitalization of one or more employees, an amputation, or loss of an eye from a work-related incident must be reported to OSHA within 24 hours (1904.39(a)(2)). Fatalities must be reported within 8 hours (1904.39(a)(1)). Workplace example: a press operator's fingertip amputation at 2 p.m. Tuesday must be reported by 2 p.m. Wednesday.

test.question: Under 1904.41(c), by what date must establishments required to submit records electronically submit them?
options: March 2 of the year after the calendar year covered by the forms
January 31
February 1 of the year after the calendar year covered, when 300-A posting begins
April 30
test.explanation: Establishments required to submit under 1904.41(a)(1) or (2) must submit by March 2 of the year after the calendar year covered (for example, March 2, 2024 for 2023 forms) (1904.41(c)). An establishment with 250 or more employees that must keep records submits 300-A information annually (1904.41(a)(1)(ii)). Workplace example: a 300-employee plant uploads its 300-A data by March 2.

title: Occupational Noise and Hearing Conservation
topics: Action level and hearing conservation programs

resources.title: Occupational Noise Exposure Standard
resources.description: Full text of 29 CFR 1910.95 on osha.gov

resources.description: Current official text of the occupational noise standard

resources.title: Occupational Noise Exposure Topic Page
resources.description: OSHA overview and guidance on noise and hearing conservation

test.question: Under 1910.95(c)(1)-(2), when must an employer administer a continuing, effective hearing conservation program?
options: Only when exposure exceeds 90 dBA
Whenever employee noise exposure equals or exceeds an 8-hour TWA of 85 dBA (or a 50% dose), which is the action level
Only after an employee reports hearing loss
Only in facilities with more than 50 employees
test.explanation: A hearing conservation program is required whenever exposures equal or exceed an 8-hour TWA of 85 dBA (slow response), or equivalently a dose of 50% (1910.95(c)(1)). That level is the action level (1910.95(c)(2)). Workplace example: stamping-line operators with a measured TWA of 87 dBA are enrolled in the program.

test.question: Under 1910.95(b)(1), what must be used first when sound levels exceed Table G-16?
options: Personal protective equipment such as earplugs or earmuffs; administrative or engineering controls are added only if protectors fail to reduce levels within the table
Shorter breaks only
Feasible administrative or engineering controls; personal protective equipment is used if they fail to reduce levels within the table
Nothing until an employee's annual audiogram shows a standard threshold shift, then hearing protectors and refitting for that employee only
test.explanation: When employees are exposed above Table G-16, feasible administrative or engineering controls must be used. If they fail to reduce sound levels within the table, PPE must be provided and used (1910.95(b)(1)). Workplace example: an enclosure is built around the blower before relying on earmuffs.

test.question: Under 1910.95(d)(1), when must the employer develop and implement a noise monitoring program?
options: Only after an OSHA inspection
Every 5 years regardless of exposure
Only when a new building is built
When information indicates any employee's exposure may equal or exceed an 8-hour TWA of 85 decibels
test.explanation: When information indicates that any employee's exposure may equal or exceed an 8-hour TWA of 85 decibels, the employer must develop and implement a monitoring program (1910.95(d)(1)). Monitoring must be repeated when changes may expose more employees at or above the action level, or make hearing protector attenuation inadequate (1910.95(d)(3)). Workplace example: a new chipper prompts dosimetry on nearby workers.

test.question: Under 1910.95(e), which employees must be notified of their monitoring results?
options: Each employee exposed at or above an 8-hour TWA of 85 decibels
All employees in the plant
Each employee exposed at or above an 8-hour TWA of 90 decibels, the permissible exposure limit
Only the supervisor of each monitored area
test.explanation: The employer must notify each employee exposed at or above an 8-hour TWA of 85 decibels of the monitoring results (1910.95(e)). Employees or their representatives must also have the chance to observe measurements (1910.95(f)). Workplace example: dosimetry results are handed to each operator measured at 86 dBA or more.

test.question: Under 1910.95(g)(5)(i), how soon after first exposure at or above the action level must a valid baseline audiogram be established (without the mobile-van exception)?
options: Within 30 days
Within 6 months
Within 1 year of exposure
Within 2 years
test.explanation: A valid baseline audiogram must be established within 6 months of first exposure at or above the action level (1910.95(g)(5)(i)). Where mobile test vans are used, it may be within 1 year, with hearing protectors worn after 6 months until the baseline is obtained (1910.95(g)(5)(ii)). Workplace example: a new hire on the press line gets a baseline within their first 6 months.

test.question: What must precede a baseline audiogram under 1910.95(g)(5)(iii)?
options: A 1-hour quiet period
A full medical exam
At least 14 hours without exposure to workplace noise (hearing protectors may substitute)
A full work shift at typical noise exposure
test.explanation: Baseline testing must be preceded by at least 14 hours without exposure to workplace noise. Hearing protectors may substitute for that quiet period (1910.95(g)(5)(iii)). Employees must also be told to avoid high non-occupational noise during the 14 hours before the test (1910.95(g)(5)(iv)). Workplace example: the baseline is scheduled first thing Monday morning after the weekend.

test.question: Under 1910.95(g)(6), how often must a new audiogram be obtained for each employee exposed at or above an 8-hour TWA of 85 decibels?
options: Every 5 years
Only when the employee reports hearing difficulty
At least every 3 years after the baseline audiogram
At least annually after the baseline
test.explanation: At least annually after the baseline audiogram, the employer must obtain a new audiogram for each employee exposed at or above an 8-hour TWA of 85 decibels (1910.95(g)(6)). Each annual audiogram is compared to the baseline (1910.95(g)(7)(i)). Workplace example: the mobile test van returns each year for the annual tests.

test.question: How does 1910.95(g)(10)(i) define a standard threshold shift?
options: A change in hearing threshold relative to baseline averaging 10 dB or more at 2000, 3000, and 4000 Hz in either ear
Any change in hearing threshold relative to the baseline audiogram at any single test frequency from 500 to 6000 Hz in either ear
A hearing loss of 25 dB or more above audiometric zero at 1000 Hz alone, measured in the worse ear on the annual audiogram
A change in hearing threshold relative to the baseline audiogram averaging 25 dB or more at 500, 1000, and 2000 Hz in both ears
test.explanation: A standard threshold shift is a change in hearing threshold relative to the baseline audiogram averaging 10 dB or more at 2000, 3000, and 4000 Hz in either ear (1910.95(g)(10)(i)). Workplace example: an employee's right ear shows an average 12 dB shift across those three frequencies, which is a standard threshold shift.

test.question: If an annual audiogram shows a standard threshold shift, within how many days must the employee be informed in writing under 1910.95(g)(8)(i)?
options: 7 working days
21 days
30 days
90 calendar days
test.explanation: If comparison shows a standard threshold shift, the employee must be informed in writing within 21 days of the determination (1910.95(g)(8)(i)). A retest within 30 days may be used as the annual audiogram (1910.95(g)(7)(ii)). Workplace example: the program coordinator mails the notice within three weeks of the audiologist's review.

test.question: What does 1910.95(i) require for hearing protectors?
options: Employees buy their own
They must be available at no cost only to employees exposed to an 8-hour TWA of 90 dB or greater, and the employer may issue a single type of protector if it is adequately rated for the noise
They must be available at no cost to all employees exposed to an 8-hour TWA of 85 dB or greater, and employees must be able to choose from a variety of suitable protectors
Only for employees above 100 dB
test.explanation: Hearing protectors must be made available at no cost to all employees exposed to an 8-hour TWA of 85 dB or greater, and replaced as necessary (1910.95(i)(1)). Employees must be able to select from a variety of suitable protectors provided by the employer (1910.95(i)(3)). Workplace example: the dispenser offers foam plugs, banded plugs, and earmuffs.

test.question: Under 1910.95(k)(2), how often must hearing conservation training be repeated?
options: Every three years, or sooner if an employee's annual audiogram shows a standard threshold shift
Only at hire
Only after a threshold shift is found on the employee's annual audiogram
Annually for each employee in the hearing conservation program
test.explanation: The training program must be repeated annually for each employee in the hearing conservation program, with information updated for changes in protective equipment and work processes (1910.95(k)(2)). It must cover the effects of noise, protectors, and audiometric testing (1910.95(k)(3)). Workplace example: the annual refresher includes the new earmuffs issued this year.

test.question: Under 1910.95(m)(3), how long must noise exposure measurement records and audiometric test records be kept?
options: Exposure measurements for 2 years; audiometric records for the duration of the affected employee's employment
Both for 30 years
Both for 1 year
Exposure measurements for the duration of employment plus 30 years; audiometric test records for 5 years after each test
test.explanation: Noise exposure measurement records must be kept for 2 years (1910.95(m)(3)(i)). Audiometric test records must be kept for the duration of the affected employee's employment (1910.95(m)(3)(ii)). Workplace example: dosimetry files older than 2 years may be purged, but an active employee's audiograms stay on file.

Quantities allowed outside cabinets or rooms

test.question: Under 1910.106(d)(2)(i), what containers may be used to store flammable liquids in container and portable tank storage?
options: Any clean container
Only approved containers and portable tanks (DOT-compliant metal containers and portable tanks are acceptable)
Glass jars
Open buckets
test.explanation: Only approved containers and portable tanks may be used. Metal containers and portable tanks meeting DOT regulations (49 CFR chapter I) are deemed acceptable (1910.106(d)(2)(i)). Workplace example: solvent is kept in its DOT drum or an approved safety can, not a coffee can.

test.question: Under 1910.106(d)(3)(i), how much flammable liquid may be stored in a single storage cabinet?
options: Not more than 25 gallons of any category in one cabinet, with containers no larger than 5 gallons each
Not more than 120 gallons of Category 1, 2, or 3, nor more than 60 gallons of Category 4 in any one cabinet
Not more than 60 gallons of Category 1, 2, or 3, nor more than 120 gallons of Category 4
250 gallons
test.explanation: Not more than 60 gallons of Category 1, 2, or 3 flammable liquids, nor more than 120 gallons of Category 4, may be stored in a storage cabinet (1910.106(d)(3)(i)). Workplace example: the paint shop cabinet holds 55 gallons of thinners and stays under the 60-gallon limit.

test.question: Under 1910.106(d)(3)(ii), what fire performance must a storage cabinet meet?
options: Limit internal temperature to 325 °F during a 5-minute fire test
Limit internal temperature to not more than 500 °F during a 30-minute fire test on the standard curve
Withstand a 2-hour fire test with internal temperature held below 212 °F at the top shelf
Limit internal temperature to not more than 325 °F during a 10-minute fire test
test.explanation: Storage cabinets must be designed and built to limit internal temperature to not more than 325 °F when subjected to a 10-minute fire test using the standard time-temperature curve (1910.106(d)(3)(ii)). Workplace example: the replacement cabinet purchased is listed as meeting the 10-minute test.

test.question: What does 1910.106(d)(5)(i) prohibit?
options: Storing flammable liquids, including stock for sale, so as to limit use of exits, stairways, or areas normally used for safe egress
Storing more than 25 gallons of flammable liquids within 10 feet of exits; smaller amounts of stock for sale may be kept in stairways and egress areas
Using safety cans
Storing flammable liquids in approved storage cabinets in a storeroom, holding no more than 60 gallons of Category 1, 2, or 3 liquids per cabinet
test.explanation: Flammable liquids, including stock for sale, may not be stored so as to limit use of exits, stairways, or areas normally used for safe egress (1910.106(d)(5)(i)). Workplace example: drums staged in the corridor to the fire exit are moved to the storage room.

test.question: Under 1910.106(d)(5)(iii), what flammable liquid storage is allowed in office occupancies?
options: Unlimited storage in desk drawers

Only what is required for building maintenance and equipment operation, kept in closed metal containers in a storage cabinet, in safety cans, or in an inside storage room not opening into public areas
Up to 10 gallons per floor in any closed container
Up to 60 gallons anywhere
test.explanation: In office occupancies, storage is prohibited except that required for maintenance and operation of the building and equipment. That storage must be in closed metal containers in a storage cabinet, in safety cans, or in an inside storage room without a door opening into the portion of the building used by the public (1910.106(d)(5)(iii)). Workplace example: the generator's fuel is kept in a safety can in the mechanical room, not the lobby.

test.question: Under 1910.106(d)(7)(i)(a), where must a portable fire extinguisher be located for a room used for flammable liquid storage?
options: Inside the room at the back
Within 100 feet anywhere
Outside the room, not more than 10 feet from the door, rated not less than 12-B units
Outside the room, within 50 feet of the door
test.explanation: At least one portable fire extinguisher rated not less than 12-B units must be located outside of, but not more than 10 feet from, the door of any room used for storage (1910.106(d)(7)(i)(a)). Workplace example: a 12-B (or higher) extinguisher hangs just outside the solvent room door.

test.question: For a Category 1, 2, or 3 flammable liquid storage area inside a building but outside a storage room, where must a 12-B extinguisher be placed under 1910.106(d)(7)(i)(b)?
options: Mounted within 5 feet of the storage area so it can be reached immediately
At least 50 feet away so the user is not exposed to a fire at the storage area
Anywhere in the building, as long as travel distance to it does not exceed 75 feet
Not less than 10 feet nor more than 25 feet from the storage area
test.explanation: At least one extinguisher rated not less than 12-B units must be located not less than 10 feet, nor more than 25 feet, from any Category 1, 2, or 3 flammable liquid storage area outside a storage room but inside a building (1910.106(d)(7)(i)(b)). Workplace example: the extinguisher for the maintenance shop's fuel can area hangs 15 feet away, not right next to it.

test.question: What does 1910.106(d)(7)(iii) say about flammable liquid storage areas?
options: Open flames and smoking are not permitted
Smoking is allowed if a sign is posted
Open flames are allowed if an extinguisher is nearby
Only smoking is prohibited; open flames are controlled through hot work permits
test.explanation: Open flames and smoking are not permitted in flammable liquid storage areas (1910.106(d)(7)(iii)). Workplace example: the storage room door is posted "No Smoking - No Open Flames" and the rule is enforced.

test.question: In a plant where flammable liquid use is incidental to the main business, how much Category 1 flammable liquid in containers may be kept outside an inside storage room or cabinet in one fire area, under 1910.106(e)(2)(ii)(b)?
options: 10 gallons
25 gallons
60 gallons
120 gallons
test.explanation: Outside an inside storage room or storage cabinet, in a building or any one fire area, the limits are 25 gallons of Category 1 in containers, 120 gallons of Category 2, 3, or 4 in containers, and 660 gallons of Category 2, 3, or 4 in a single portable tank (1910.106(e)(2)(ii)(b)). Workplace example: the furniture plant's finishing area keeps no more than 25 gallons of Category 1 lacquer thinner out of the cabinet.

test.question: Under 1910.106(e)(2)(iv)(d), which method of transferring flammable liquids within a building is prohibited?
options: Through a closed piping system
By a device drawing through the top of the container, such as a hand-operated drum pump
By applying air pressure to the container or portable tank
By gravity through an approved self-closing valve
test.explanation: Flammable liquids may be drawn from or transferred into vessels, containers, or portable tanks inside a building only through a closed piping system, from safety cans, by a device drawing through the top, or by gravity through an approved self-closing valve. Transferring by air pressure on the container or portable tank is prohibited (1910.106(e)(2)(iv)(d)). Workplace example: a drum pump is used instead of pressurizing the drum with shop air.

test.question: Under 1910.106(e)(6)(ii), when may Category 1 or 2 flammable liquids (or Category 3 below 100 °F flashpoint) be dispensed into containers?
options: At any time
Only outdoors, where vapors disperse and no bonding of the nozzle and container is needed
Only when the receiving container is plastic, so no static spark can jump between the nozzle and container
Only when the nozzle and container are electrically interconnected
test.explanation: These liquids may not be dispensed into containers unless the nozzle and container are electrically interconnected. A metallic floorplate electrically connected to the fill stem, or a fill stem bonded to the container during filling, satisfies this (1910.106(e)(6)(ii)). Workplace example: a bonding clip connects the drum and the metal can before solvent is dispensed.

test.question: Under 1910.106(e)(2)(iv)(a), how must Category 1 or 2 flammable liquids (or Category 3 below 100 °F flashpoint) be kept at the point of final use?
options: In covered containers when not actually in use
In open pans at the workstation, covered at the end of the day
Only in glass
In any container
test.explanation: At the point of final use, these liquids must be kept in covered containers when not actually in use (1910.106(e)(2)(iv)(a)). Means must be provided to promptly and safely dispose of leaks or spills (1910.106(e)(2)(iv)(b)). Workplace example: the parts-wash solvent pail has a lid that is closed between uses.
